lessons.title: Read a Kubernetes resource
lessons.subtitle: The shape of every manifest
lessons.objective: Distinguish resource identity, desired configuration, and observed state.
lessons.context: You are reading a Pod manifest in the training project. This is a practice workspace; no cluster changes are made.
teaching: Every resource has an API version, a kind, and metadata that identifies it.
Namespaces separate namespaced resources. Labels describe resources so other objects can select them.
spec describes desired configuration. Controllers report observed state through status; editing status does not change the desired configuration.
lessons.memory_cue: Version and kind identify the API; metadata identifies the object; spec describes intent.

lab.start: Use a disposable project with one existing Pod and read-only access.
lab.task: Locate its API version, kind, namespace, labels, and container image without changing it.
lab.verify: Compare oc get pod <name> -n <project> -o yaml with oc describe pod <name> -n <project>.
lab.reset: No changes are needed for this read-only task.

lessons.title: Pods, labels & reconciliation
lessons.subtitle: Understand what a Deployment manages
lessons.objective: Connect a Deployment to its Pod template, selector, and desired replica count.
lessons.context: A catalog Deployment should maintain three Pods. The template and Deployment selector must agree.
teaching: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which maintain Pods matching their selectors.
The Deployment selector must match labels on its Pod template. Changing a template rolls out new Pods.
Replicas describe desired count; readiness and scheduling can prevent the actual ready count from matching it.
lessons.memory_cue: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Selectors and template labels must agree.

lab.start: Use a disposable project with permission to inspect a Deployment.
lab.task: Trace owner references from a Pod to a ReplicaSet and then its Deployment.
lab.verify: Inspect oc get deployment,rs,pods -n <project> and compare selectors with Pod template labels.
lab.reset: This task is read-only; do not delete production Pods to test reconciliation.

lessons.title: Connect Services to Pods
lessons.subtitle: Labels, ports & ready endpoints
lessons.objective: Trace Service selection and distinguish the Service port from the application target port.
lessons.context: Catalog Pods in training have app=catalog and listen on 8080. Clients use Service port 80. The Pods have no special hostname or subdomain requirements.
teaching: A Service selector compares labels on Pods in the same namespace; it does not match a Deployment name automatically.
port is the client-facing Service port. targetPort is the backend application port or named Pod port.
EndpointSlices describe matching backends and their conditions. Running alone does not establish readiness. A Route adds external routing to a Service.
lessons.memory_cue: Selectors choose Pods. targetPort chooses their application port. Readiness decides normal traffic eligibility.

lab.start: Use a disposable project with a working HTTP Deployment and Service.
lab.task: Compare Pod labels, Service selectors, ports, and ready EndpointSlices before testing the application.
lab.verify: Run oc get pods --show-labels, oc get svc catalog -o yaml, and oc get endpointslice -l kubernetes.io/service-name=catalog in the same project.
lab.reset: Restore any edited selector from the saved original manifest; verify endpoints recover.

lessons.title: Wire application configuration
lessons.subtitle: ConfigMaps, Secrets & references
lessons.objective: Read environment references and choose configuration resources for their intended purpose.
lessons.context: The catalog application reads LOG_LEVEL from a ConfigMap called catalog-config. Credentials must be managed separately using a Secret and appropriate access controls.
teaching: ConfigMaps store non-confidential settings. Secrets are intended for confidential values but still require access control and suitable storage protection.
A key reference identifies both the source object and its key in the same namespace.
Environment variables are set when the container starts. Updating a ConfigMap does not rewrite the environment in an existing process. Base64 is encoding, not encryption.
lessons.memory_cue: Reference the object and the key. Environment changes need a new container start.

lab.start: Use a disposable project and a sample app that prints non-sensitive configuration.
lab.task: Create a ConfigMap, reference one key in a workload, and observe an environment value before and after replacing its Pods.
lab.verify: Compare the ConfigMap key with the Pod environment reference; never print real credentials as part of verification.
lab.reset: Remove only the sample workload and ConfigMap you created in the disposable project.

lessons.title: Health checks & capacity
lessons.subtitle: Ready is different from running
lessons.objective: Distinguish readiness, liveness, requests, and limits when diagnosing workload behaviour.
lessons.context: Catalog listens on 8080. /ready indicates traffic readiness; /live indicates whether restarting could help. The application needs a 100m CPU scheduling request and a 256Mi memory limit for this exercise.
teaching: Readiness failures remove normal traffic eligibility; liveness failures can trigger a container restart after their threshold.
Startup probes can protect slow initialisation from premature liveness checks.
Requests influence scheduling. Limits constrain resource usage. A Running Pod may still be unready or restarting.
lessons.memory_cue: Readiness controls traffic; liveness can restart; requests inform placement.

lab.start: Use a disposable HTTP workload with documented health endpoints.
lab.task: Inspect readiness, liveness, resource requests, and recent container termination reasons.
lab.verify: Compare oc describe pod <name> with its probe configuration, events, and container status; distinguish Pending from OOMKilled.
lab.reset: Restore the original probes and resources if changed; wait for a healthy rollout.

lessons.title: Request persistent storage
lessons.subtitle: Claims, classes & mounts
lessons.objective: Connect a PVC request to a StorageClass, binding, and workload mount.
lessons.context: A sample workload needs a 1Gi filesystem claim named catalog-data using the existing lab-storage StorageClass. This lab assumes that class supports ReadWriteOnce.
teaching: A PVC requests storage. A PV represents storage capacity. A StorageClass describes provisioning choices.
Binding a claim and mounting it in a running Pod are separate steps. Pending needs events and class/capacity checks.
ReadWriteOnce concerns read-write mounting on one node; it does not mean exactly one Pod. Retention depends on reclaim policy and the storage system.
lessons.memory_cue: Claim requests; class provisions; volume backs; Pod mounts.

lab.start: Use a disposable project with a known working StorageClass; expect possible storage charges in hosted labs.
lab.task: Create a small claim, inspect binding events, and mount it in a sample workload.
lab.verify: Inspect oc get pvc,pv and oc describe pvc catalog-data; write a sample file and verify it survives replacement of the sample Pod.
lab.reset: Remove the sample workload and claim; inspect the PV reclaim policy and verify disposal of only the lab storage.

lessons.title: Identities & least privilege
lessons.subtitle: Roles bind permissions to subjects
lessons.objective: Read a namespaced RoleBinding and distinguish API permissions from workload security constraints.
lessons.context: The existing Role pod-reader grants read-only Pod access in training. Bind it to the existing inspector ServiceAccount in training without granting cluster-wide access.
teaching: A Role defines namespaced permissions. A RoleBinding associates a Role or ClusterRole with subjects within the binding namespace.
ServiceAccounts are workload identities. RBAC authorisation and SCC admission answer different questions.
OpenShift SCCs constrain workload security settings. Prefer compatible images and minimal permissions over granting privileged access.
lessons.memory_cue: Roles define actions; bindings connect subjects; SCCs constrain workload security.

lab.start: Use a disposable project and an administrator-approved read-only Role and ServiceAccount.
lab.task: Inspect a RoleBinding and compare the subject with the Role rules before testing access.
lab.verify: If authorised to impersonate, use oc auth can-i get pods --as=system:serviceaccount:training:inspector -n training; inspect the Role rules too.
lab.reset: Delete only your sample binding; do not alter cluster roles or default SCCs.

lessons.title: Placement & network isolation
lessons.subtitle: Scheduling and connectivity are separate
lessons.objective: Interpret a node selector and recognise what scheduling constraints can and cannot do.
lessons.context: The catalog Pod must run on a node labelled workload=apps and disk=ssd. It uses the existing catalog-data claim; assume suitable storage topology and node capacity for the YAML examples.
teaching: Node selectors constrain which labelled nodes are eligible. Requests and storage topology can constrain placement further.
Tolerations permit matching taints; they do not force placement or bypass node affinity.
NetworkPolicy controls supported network traffic rules. It does not create CPU capacity or move a Pod onto a node.
lessons.memory_cue: Labels constrain placement; tolerations permit taints; policies constrain traffic.

lab.start: Use a disposable workload and inspect existing node labels without changing shared node labels.
lab.task: Compare a workload node selector with actual labels and scheduler events.
lab.verify: Inspect oc get nodes --show-labels and oc describe pod <name>; separately inspect applicable NetworkPolicies for a traffic failure.
lab.reset: Restore only the sample workload selector if you changed it.

lessons.title: Read evidence before changing things
lessons.subtitle: Events, conditions & supplied output
lessons.objective: Use workload evidence to choose the next diagnostic check and a bounded repair.
lessons.context: A batch validation Job should run once, retry at most twice, and clean up one hour after finishing. Output shown in questions is supplied practice evidence, not live command execution.
teaching: Read desired configuration, current conditions, recent events, and container state together.
Logs explain application behaviour; events explain scheduling, image pulls, mounts, and health check failures.
Jobs run tasks to completion. Retry and cleanup settings express different lifecycle choices.
lessons.memory_cue: Configuration → conditions → events → logs → smallest justified change.

lab.start: Use a disposable project with an intentionally failing sample Job and its known expected behaviour.
lab.task: Inspect events, container status, and logs; record a diagnosis before editing the Job template.
lab.verify: Compare oc describe job <name>, oc describe pod <name>, and oc logs <pod>; verify a corrected sample task completes.
lab.reset: Remove only the sample Jobs and Pods; retain the diagnostic notes.

lessons.title: Safe operations & recovery
lessons.subtitle: Build a bridge to advanced administration
lessons.objective: Distinguish availability, reconciliation, and recovery evidence before attempting advanced scenarios.
lessons.context: The catalog Deployment normally has three ready replicas. Use a PodDisruptionBudget allowing at least two healthy selected Pods during voluntary disruptions. This is a foundations bridge, not a complete EX380 syllabus.
teaching: A PodDisruptionBudget constrains supported voluntary evictions. It does not prevent all outages or replace replica capacity.
GitOps controllers reconcile declared configuration; manual edits may be reverted. Identify the source of truth before changing managed objects.
A successful backup job is not proof of recoverability. Restore into an isolated environment and verify application data and dependencies.
lessons.memory_cue: Availability needs capacity; GitOps needs a source of truth; recovery needs a tested restore.

lab.start: Use an isolated training environment and a sample app with non-sensitive data; record its baseline.
lab.task: Write a restore rehearsal checklist that includes workload resources, data, secrets, external endpoints, and application validation.
lab.verify: Restore only in the isolated environment, validate sample data and dependencies, and record actual recovery evidence separately from quiz results.
lab.reset: Remove only rehearsal resources; verify that external integrations were never pointed at production services.

lessons.title: Routes, TLS & request paths
lessons.objective: Choose a TLS termination mode and trace a request through the router to its backend.
teaching: Edge termination ends TLS at the router; re-encrypt starts a second TLS connection to the backend; passthrough leaves termination to the backend.
Route targetPort resolves a Service port. Service targetPort then resolves the Pod listener.
A certificate proves identity only when the chain and expected name can be verified. A healthy Route also needs ready backends.
lessons.memory_cue: Client TLS and backend TLS are separate connections in re-encrypt mode.

lab.start: Disposable TLS application, Service and test certificates.
lab.task: Compare edge and re-encrypt paths without bypassing verification.
lab.verify: Inspect Route admitted conditions, Service ports, ready EndpointSlices and backend certificate chain; test using the correct CA.
lab.reset: Remove only the test Route and restore the saved Service.

lessons.subtitle: Application exposure and TLS

lessons.title: NetworkPolicy & DNS
lessons.objective: Evaluate additive network rules, selector scope and the DNS dependency of isolated Pods.
teaching: Policies are additive. Once a direction is isolated, traffic must match an allowed rule from at least one selecting policy.
A podSelector peer without a namespaceSelector means Pods in the policy namespace. Selectors within one peer combine; separate peers are alternatives.
Egress isolation must allow required DNS traffic and application destinations. Successful DNS does not prove application connectivity.
lessons.memory_cue: One peer combines selectors; separate peers provide alternatives. Policies allow traffic rather than creating routes.

lab.start: Disposable API and client Pods with known labels and DNS working.
lab.task: Test allowed and disallowed clients; add DNS egress explicitly if introducing egress isolation.
lab.verify: Record source namespace and labels, destination port, policy selectors and connection results.
lab.reset: Remove only the lab policies; confirm baseline DNS and HTTP work.

lessons.subtitle: Pod traffic isolation

lessons.title: Quotas, defaults & admission
lessons.objective: Distinguish project quotas, per-container limits and scheduler requests.
teaching: ResourceQuota caps aggregate consumption in a namespace; LimitRange can constrain or default individual resource requests and limits.
Admission rejection happens before scheduling. Pending from insufficient node capacity is a different failure.
Terminating or unready objects may still count toward applicable quotas; inspect reported used and hard values.
lessons.memory_cue: Quota limits namespace totals; LimitRange shapes individual requests; the scheduler places admitted Pods.

lab.start: Disposable project with a saved quota and no production workloads.
lab.task: Observe an admission rejection and compare quota used/hard with a pending scheduling failure.
lab.verify: Inspect oc describe quota and Pod or ReplicaSet events; confirm the failure stage.
lab.reset: Restore the original quota and remove sample workloads.

lessons.subtitle: Project resource governance

lessons.title: HPA & rollout capacity
lessons.objective: Read CPU-based autoscaling and distinguish desired replicas from ready capacity.
teaching: CPU utilisation is measured relative to resource requests, not CPU limits.
HPA adjusts desired replica count; scheduling, startup and readiness still determine usable capacity.
A GitOps replica declaration can compete with an HPA unless ownership and diff handling are designed explicitly.
lessons.memory_cue: Metrics decide desired scale; requests define utilisation; scheduling and readiness decide usable scale.

lab.start: Disposable Deployment with resource requests and working metrics.
lab.task: Inspect autoscaling conditions under controlled sample load.
lab.verify: Compare oc get hpa, oc describe hpa and Deployment desired/ready replicas; inspect metrics availability.
lab.reset: Stop the load generator and restore the sample autoscaling configuration.

lessons.subtitle: Application scaling and availability

lessons.title: Operators & reconciliation
lessons.objective: Distinguish a CRD, a custom resource, an Operator and its installation lifecycle.
teaching: A CRD adds an API type; a custom resource is an instance of that type. The Operator reconciles instances into managed components.
A Subscription selects a package and channel. InstallPlans describe changes; a CSV reports an installed Operator version and its requirements.
Installation success does not establish that every managed application instance is healthy. Inspect each resource’s conditions.
lessons.memory_cue: Subscription selects; InstallPlan installs; CSV reports Operator state; custom resources declare managed intent.

lab.start: Disposable Operator namespace, approved catalog and supported package/channel.
lab.task: Inspect Subscription, OperatorGroup, InstallPlan and CSV before creating a sample custom resource.
lab.verify: Compare install scope, approved plan, CSV conditions, CRD discovery and sample resource status.
lab.reset: Delete the sample instance before uninstalling lab-only Operator resources; follow its supported cleanup procedure.

lessons.subtitle: Operator lifecycle and custom resources

lessons.title: Images, builds & deployment inputs
lessons.objective: Distinguish tags, digests, image pull credentials and build-time versus runtime configuration.
teaching: Tags are mutable references; a digest identifies a specific image manifest or index. Architecture selection can still matter for an image index.
Image pull credentials are referenced by the Pod or its ServiceAccount; build credentials and runtime application credentials have different roles.
BuildConfig/Build produce images; Deployments run them. A successful build is not evidence of a healthy rollout.
lessons.memory_cue: Build produces; registry stores; digest identifies; workload runs.

lab.start: Disposable app, approved accessible image, test registry credentials and optional BuildConfig.
lab.task: Inspect image provenance, build logs and the Pod image pull reference separately.
lab.verify: Compare declared image reference with container status imageID, pull events and the resulting rollout health.
lab.reset: Remove sample build outputs and workload references; revoke lab-only credentials.

lessons.subtitle: Image provenance and application delivery

lessons.title: OAuth, OIDC & kubeconfig
lessons.objective: Separate identity-provider login, identity mapping, API credentials and RBAC authorisation.
teaching: An identity provider authenticates a user; RBAC then authorises that identity. Neither substitutes for the other.
OAuth configuration is cluster-scoped. Provider names, mapping methods and identity claims affect how users are linked.
A kubeconfig combines cluster trust, credentials and context. Expired tokens, wrong contexts and missing permissions are different failures.
lessons.memory_cue: Authenticate the identity, map it deliberately, then authorise only the required actions.

lab.start: Isolated cluster, test OIDC client and a retained working administrator login.
lab.task: Inspect discovery, Secret reference, claims and a restricted user kubeconfig before changing authentication.
lab.verify: Test login and oc whoami, then verify one allowed and one denied API action using the actual user credentials.
lab.reset: Restore saved OAuth configuration and revoke only lab credentials; retain the administrator recovery path.

lessons.subtitle: Federated identity and API authentication

lessons.title: LDAP groups & scheduled sync
lessons.objective: Plan scheduled directory synchronisation and verify actual group-based permissions.
teaching: LDAP login and LDAP group synchronisation are separate processes. Membership removals must be propagated and verified.
A dry run previews sync changes; --confirm applies them. Pruning orphaned groups is a separate reviewed operation.
CronJob concurrency and credential rotation matter. Impersonating a manually supplied group cannot prove the actual directory membership.
lessons.memory_cue: Directory membership → synchronised Group → binding → effective permissions.

lab.start: Test directory group, isolated sync configuration and a verified administrative recovery account.
lab.task: Preview additions/removals, apply the reviewed sync and test actual users with a namespaced binding.
lab.verify: Compare directory membership, OpenShift Group users, CronJob execution history and allowed/denied actions using fresh actual user credentials.
lab.reset: Remove the lab schedule and role binding, revoke test bind credentials and restore the saved test group.

lessons.subtitle: Group lifecycle and delegated access

lessons.title: OADP backup & restore
lessons.objective: Distinguish metadata export, backup scope, volume protection and a tested application restore.
teaching: YAML export does not contain image layers or application data in volumes or external services.
Backup success depends on included namespaces, selectors, storage methods, credentials and completed volume protection.
A restore must be isolated from production integrations and validated using application data and dependency checks.
lessons.memory_cue: Scope the resources, protect the data, then prove an isolated restore.

lab.start: Isolated sample data, working OADP installation and approved backup/snapshot storage.
lab.task: Back up sample resources and supported data, restore to an isolated target and disable real integrations.
lab.verify: Inspect Backup/Restore conditions and volume operations; verify known data and application functionality in the restored target.
lab.reset: Remove only rehearsal resources and test backups according to retention policy; do not delete production backup locations.

lessons.subtitle: Application resources

lessons.title: MachineConfigPools & node changes
lessons.objective: Predict the scope and operational impact of a MachineConfig and read pool rollout evidence.
teaching: MachineConfigPool selectors determine which MachineConfigs are rendered together and which nodes receive the result.
Machine configuration changes may drain and reboot nodes. Node placement, workload availability and rollback planning must be reviewed first.
Degraded pool state needs node and daemon evidence, not just another configuration edit. Direct host drift can break reconciliation.
lessons.memory_cue: Determine the selected pool and nodes before assessing the drain/reboot blast radius.

lab.start: Dedicated disposable worker pool, saved configuration and approved reboot budget.
lab.task: Inspect selectors and pool conditions; plan an innocuous lab file change before applying it.
lab.verify: Compare rendered/current/desired configurations, pool Updated/Updating/Degraded conditions and MachineConfigDaemon evidence.
lab.reset: Use the supported declarative rollback and wait for pool convergence; verify the node file and workload health.

lessons.subtitle: Cluster partitioning and machine configuration

lessons.title: Dedicated nodes & disruption budgets
lessons.objective: Combine taints, tolerations and required placement without confusing permission with attraction.
teaching: A toleration permits a matching taint but does not attract the Pod to that node. A selector or affinity rule supplies the required placement.
NoSchedule affects new placement, while NoExecute can affect existing Pods unless tolerated appropriately.
PDBs constrain supported voluntary evictions; required anti-affinity and storage topology can limit replacement capacity.
lessons.memory_cue: Tolerate the taint and select the node; then verify capacity to survive disruption.

lab.start: Disposable labelled worker nodes, sample workload and approved test taint.
lab.task: Predict eligible nodes before applying selectors and tolerations; assess a voluntary eviction against a sample PDB.
lab.verify: Compare node labels/taints, Pod constraints, scheduling events and PDB disruptionsAllowed.
lab.reset: Remove only the test taint and restore the sample workload constraints.

lessons.subtitle: Placement

lessons.title: GitOps, Helm & Kustomize
lessons.objective: Reason about GitOps ownership, destination boundaries, rendering and destructive reconciliation.
teaching: GitOps reconciles declared state. Sync, health and drift are different properties.
AppProject and destination permissions limit what an Application can manage; repository access and cluster permissions are separate boundaries.
Helm values and Kustomize overlays render manifests. Inspect rendered output, especially namespace, storage and deletion scope.
lessons.memory_cue: Review rendered intent, allowed destination and deletion behaviour before sync.

lab.start: Isolated Argo CD instance/project and a test repository with no production credentials.
lab.task: Render the overlay, inspect the resource diff and test an intentional drift correction on a disposable workload.
lab.verify: Compare Git revision, destination, rendered objects, sync status and health; verify PVC deletion policy separately.
lab.reset: Disable auto-sync before removing lab applications and preserve or explicitly dispose of test data according to policy.

lessons.subtitle: Declarative fleet and application management

lessons.title: Metrics, ServiceMonitors & alerts
lessons.objective: Trace metric discovery, scrape access, alert evaluation and notification as separate stages.
teaching: ServiceMonitor selectors choose Services; endpoints.port refers to a Service port name. PodMonitor is a separate direct-Pod discovery mechanism.
Target discovery, network access, TLS, authentication and metric content can fail independently.
Alert expressions and for durations determine firing; notification routing and silences determine delivery. A silence does not repair the underlying fault.
lessons.memory_cue: Discover → scrape → evaluate → notify. Verify each boundary independently.

lab.start: Disposable metrics Service and enabled user-workload monitoring.
lab.task: Create a ServiceMonitor, inspect the target and test a temporary alert and scoped expiring silence.
lab.verify: Compare Service labels/port names, target scrape errors, returned series, alert state and receiver delivery.
lab.reset: Remove the test rule/monitor and expire the test silence; restore the application configuration.

lessons.subtitle: Monitoring

lessons.title: Vector forwarding, Loki & retention
lessons.objective: Trace logging inputs, authorised collection, pipelines, receiver transport and retention.
teaching: Logging 6 uses observability.openshift.io/v1 ClusterLogForwarder; legacy APIs are not interchangeable.
Inputs choose log sources, pipelines connect those inputs to named outputs, and the ServiceAccount requires explicit collection permissions.
Vector collection/forwarding and Loki storage/query/retention are separate components. Receiver backpressure and storage health need their own evidence.
lessons.memory_cue: Authorised input → pipeline → output → receiver/storage → query and retention.

lab.start: Disposable Logging 6 configuration, authorised collector and controlled external receiver.
lab.task: Forward a uniquely marked application log, then trace it through collector and receiver evidence.
lab.verify: Inspect ClusterLogForwarder conditions, collector permissions/logs, receiver response and query results; verify retention on the storage system separately.
lab.reset: Restore the prior forwarder configuration and remove only test receiver credentials and log-generation workloads.

lessons.subtitle: Log collection

lessons.title: Shell tools, text & archives
lessons.objective: Choose exact shell, redirection, text-search, archive and SSH syntax without confusing options or expansion.
teaching: The shell processes redirection and quoting before a command runs; ordering of file-descriptor duplication matters.
Search predicates, recursive scope and exact-match options change results. Inspect intended paths before mutating files.
Archives preserve selected metadata, but restore behaviour also depends on permissions and extraction options. Verify SSH host identity rather than bypassing checks.
lessons.memory_cue: Parse the shell first, then command options, then the target path.

lab.start: Disposable directory, test files and an authorised SSH test host.
lab.task: Predict output and redirections before running read-only searches and creating a sample archive.
lab.verify: Compare expected matched lines, stdout/stderr files, archive contents and verified remote host identity.
lab.reset: Remove only the created lab files after inspecting their absolute paths.

objective_groups: Essential shell tools and secure file handling
lessons.subtitle: Essential shell tools and secure file handling

lessons.title: Shell scripts & scheduled work
lessons.objective: Read quoting, conditionals, loops, exit status and scheduled execution environments.
teaching: Quote expansions used as single arguments, especially paths. Unquoted expansion can split words and expand globs.
Exit status zero means success; conditionals test status rather than whether command output is nonempty.
Cron, at and systemd timers schedule work differently. Environment, working directory, credentials and error handling must be explicit.
lessons.memory_cue: Quote inputs, test status and make scheduled execution assumptions explicit.

lab.start: Disposable Bash script, paths containing spaces and a test user timer.
lab.task: Test success and failure inputs interactively and under a scheduler.
lab.verify: Inspect argument count, exit status, absolute paths and the timer/service journal.
lab.reset: Disable and remove only the sample timer and script.

lessons.subtitle: Shell automation and task scheduling

lessons.title: systemd, journals & boot
lessons.objective: Distinguish runtime state, boot enablement, persistent journals, targets and process evidence.
teaching: Starting a service changes runtime state; enabling configures activation dependencies for later boots.
Unit-file changes need a manager reload before using updated definitions. Application configuration reload and systemd daemon-reload are different.
Journals can be queried by unit and boot. Persistent storage and retention must be configured rather than inferred from current logs.
lessons.memory_cue: Start for now, enable for boot, reload the manager for changed units.

lab.start: Disposable VM, sample service and working console access.
lab.task: Enable a service, change a drop-in, reload units and inspect journal evidence across a controlled reboot.
lab.verify: Check is-enabled, is-active, effective unit configuration and current/previous boot journal entries.
lab.reset: Remove only the lab drop-in, reload the manager and restore the original service/target settings.

objective_groups: Running systems and persistent service configuration
lessons.subtitle: Running systems and persistent service configuration

lessons.title: LVM, filesystems & persistent mounts
lessons.objective: Distinguish block devices, PV/VG/LV allocation, filesystem growth, UUID mounts and safe recovery.
teaching: A larger logical volume does not automatically mean a larger filesystem unless the filesystem is also grown.
Filesystem operations are type-specific. XFS supports online growth but not shrinking.
Persistent mounts must reference the intended device identity and be tested before reboot; NFS and automount introduce remote dependencies.
lessons.memory_cue: Block capacity → logical volume → filesystem → mount. Verify each layer.

lab.start: Disposable VM with a dedicated lab disk, verified device identity and a recoverable sample filesystem.
lab.task: Inspect PV/VG/LV capacity, grow the sample LV and XFS filesystem, and test a UUID mount entry.
lab.verify: Compare lsblk -f, pvs/vgs/lvs, findmnt and df before/after; validate mount configuration before a controlled reboot.
lab.reset: Recreate only the disposable lab storage from its baseline; do not attempt to shrink XFS.

lessons.subtitle: Local storage and filesystem lifecycle

lessons.title: Users, permissions & privilege
lessons.objective: Read group membership, permission inheritance and scoped administrative access.
teaching: Supplementary groups are additive; usermod -G without -a replaces the supplementary group list.
Directory write and execute permissions control creation/removal and traversal. File permissions alone do not decide deletion from a directory.
Setgid directories influence group inheritance; sticky directories constrain deletion by other users. Sudo policy must be reviewed and syntax-checked.
lessons.memory_cue: Identity → group membership → directory traversal → file access → explicit privilege.

lab.start: Disposable test accounts, group and directory; retain an authorised administrator session.
lab.task: Configure additive group membership and a setgid shared directory, then test with fresh user sessions.
lab.verify: Inspect id, directory mode/ownership, new-file group ownership and the intended sudo command scope.
lab.reset: Remove only sample accounts/policy entries and restore saved lab-directory permissions.

lessons.subtitle: Local identities

lessons.title: SELinux labels & persistent policy
lessons.objective: Distinguish DAC permissions, SELinux labels, persistent context mappings, port types and booleans.
teaching: SELinux applies mandatory policy in addition to ordinary permissions. Enforcing denies disallowed operations; permissive records them without enforcing those denials.
semanage fcontext persists pathname-to-context rules; restorecon applies the expected context. A one-time chcon is not the same as a persistent policy mapping.
Port labels and booleans adjust specific policy behaviour. Diagnose AVCs and use the narrow supported change rather than disabling enforcement.
lessons.memory_cue: Inspect the denial, define the intended persistent label, then restore and retest.

lab.start: Disposable web service with SELinux enforcing and a custom document root.
lab.task: Diagnose a controlled label mismatch and apply a reviewed persistent context mapping.
lab.verify: Inspect ls -Z, matchpathcon, relevant AVCs and application access after restorecon and a controlled relabel test.
lab.reset: Remove only the custom lab mapping and restore the original service/document-root configuration.

objective_groups: Mandatory access control and host security
lessons.subtitle: Mandatory access control and host security

lessons.title: NetworkManager, DNS & firewalld
lessons.objective: Distinguish connection profiles, active addresses, DNS resolution and runtime/permanent firewall rules.
teaching: Editing a connection profile and activating it are separate actions; current device state may differ from saved configuration.
DNS resolution, routing, listening sockets and firewall policy are distinct boundaries.
firewalld runtime and permanent configurations are separate. Zone selection must match the interface/source that carries the traffic.
lessons.memory_cue: Saved profile → active link/address → route/DNS → listener → firewall path.

lab.start: Disposable VM with console access, known connection profile and saved network settings.
lab.task: Inspect active versus saved settings and test a narrowly scoped firewall service in the actual active zone.
lab.verify: Compare nmcli, ip route, getent hosts, ss listeners and runtime/permanent firewall queries before a controlled reboot.
lab.reset: Restore the saved profile and remove only the test firewall rule; verify access from the console.

objective_groups: Persistent host networking and access policy
lessons.subtitle: Persistent host networking and access policy

lessons.title: Packages, time & recovery
lessons.objective: Distinguish package sources, Flatpak scope, time synchronisation and persistent recovery changes.
teaching: DNF manages RPM repository packages and dependencies; Flatpak uses remotes and application refs with user/system scope.
An installed package is not necessarily an enabled healthy service. Time synchronisation needs actual source/offset evidence.
Recovery work must preserve filesystems and restore persistent configuration; a temporary boot change does not necessarily change the next normal boot.
lessons.memory_cue: Source and scope first; then installation, activation and verified persistence.

lab.start: Disposable VM with approved package/remotes, a trusted time source and a recovery snapshot.
lab.task: Inspect package sources and scopes, verify time synchronisation and rehearse console recovery using the designated RHEL procedure.
lab.verify: Compare repo metadata, installed RPM/Flatpak refs, service state, chrony source evidence and normal boot behaviour.
lab.reset: Remove sample applications/remotes, restore saved service settings and revert only the disposable recovery snapshot.

lessons.subtitle: Software management

lessons.title: StatefulSets, DaemonSets & batch controllers
lessons.objective: Choose controllers by lifecycle and reason about stable identity, storage and ordered startup.
teaching: StatefulSets provide stable ordinal identity and per-replica claim templates, but do not implement database replication or backups.
DaemonSets place Pods on eligible nodes; Jobs target completion; CronJobs create Jobs on a schedule.
Ordered startup and application quorum can interact. Storage and membership recovery need an application-aware procedure.
lessons.memory_cue: Choose the lifecycle controller first; then design data, identity and recovery around it.

lab.start: Disposable stateful sample, existing headless Service and supported storage.
lab.task: Observe ordinal identities and per-replica claims; compare with an eligible-node DaemonSet and a one-shot Job.
lab.verify: Inspect owner references, Pod DNS/ordinals, PVC names and application membership; record persistence separately from replication.
lab.reset: Remove lab controllers using an explicit data-retention plan and inspect remaining claims before disposal.

objective_groups: Controller choice and stateful application lifecycle
lessons.subtitle: Controller choice and stateful application lifecycle

lessons.title: Tekton pipelines & promotion boundaries
lessons.objective: Distinguish pipeline definitions, runs, execution identities, workspaces and release promotion evidence.
teaching: A Pipeline describes task relationships; PipelineRun requests an execution with parameters, workspaces and an identity.
Build registry access, source credentials and deployment rights are distinct permissions; avoid giving a build worker broad cluster administration.
Successful build execution does not authorise production promotion. Record provenance and approved immutable image identity before updating GitOps intent.
lessons.memory_cue: Definition → run inputs and identity → build evidence → approved promotion → reconciliation.

lab.start: Isolated namespace, preinstalled supported pipeline definitions and scoped registry/source credentials.
lab.task: Create a PipelineRun using the declared parameters/workspace and inspect TaskRun results without deploying to production.
lab.verify: Compare run conditions, task logs, workspace binding, execution identity and produced digest with the approved promotion record.
lab.reset: Remove only lab runs and dispose of cache claims/credentials according to policy.

lessons.subtitle: Pipeline execution and GitOps integration

lessons.title: Projects, API health & configuration scope
lessons.objective: Separate project self-service, cluster-scoped configuration and supported Operator-managed changes.
teaching: OpenShift Projects add management metadata and policy around namespaces. Project creation permission is distinct from editing a workload in one project.
Cluster-scoped configuration can affect Operators and nodes beyond one application. Use supported configuration objects rather than editing generated children.
API/server, ingress, proxy, DNS and certificate failures can present similar client symptoms; identify which connection failed before changing global settings.
lessons.memory_cue: Establish identity and scope, then inspect the supported configuration owner and affected connection.

lab.start: Isolated cluster with saved proxy/trust configuration and a tested administrator recovery path.
lab.task: Inspect project permissions and trace a test Operator egress/trust issue without changing unrelated application settings.
lab.verify: Compare supported Proxy config, referenced CA bundle, Operator conditions and verified outbound TLS connectivity.
lab.reset: Restore saved cluster configuration using the supported API and wait for affected Operators/nodes to converge.

objective_groups: Cluster configuration and delegated project administration
lessons.subtitle: Cluster configuration and delegated project administration

lessons.title: Disk provisioning, swap, NFS & autofs
lessons.objective: Choose the correct provisioning layer and distinguish active swap, persistent mounts and automount maps.
teaching: Partition tables, LVM PVs, VGs, LVs and filesystems are separate layers. Formatting the wrong layer destroys existing data.
mkswap initialises a swap area; swapon activates it; persistent configuration is a separate requirement.
An NFS mount depends on server/export, network, client access and local mount configuration. autofs maps define mounts triggered by path access.
lessons.memory_cue: Verify the device, provision the correct layer, activate it and test persistence.

lab.start: Disposable VM, verified empty lab disk, backup/recovery snapshot and authorised test NFS export.
lab.task: Plan the disk layers, add a small test LV and swap area, then compare explicit NFS mounting with an autofs map.
lab.verify: Compare lsblk, pvs/vgs/lvs, swapon --show, findmnt and mount behaviour before/after controlled reboot or path access.
lab.reset: Unmount and deactivate only lab resources before disposal; remove their persistent entries and verify original mounts still work.

openshift.scenario: The production checkout error-ratio alert fires overnight after one failed request and no other traffic. During the day, sustained failures should page promptly. The metric is a counter with status labels.
openshift.question: An error ratio with a zero denominator can be ___; a production rule therefore needs an explicit ___ policy as well as a sustained condition.

choices.explanation: Silencing permanently hides real failures instead of defining expression behavior.
Zero divided by zero is not a reliable meaningful error ratio.

The rule should distinguish quiet periods from impactful service failures.

openshift.title: Troubleshoot a route returning 503
openshift.scenario:
A new catalog release is Running, but its public route returns HTTP 503.
You have project access and must identify the fault before changing configuration.
openshift.question: Which checks are appropriate before changing a Route that returns 503?

choices.text: Scale a Deployment with a wrong Service selector and expect the selector to repair itself.
choices.explanation: Additional replicas do not correct label selection.

choices.text: Assume the router is broken because the pod phase is Running.
choices.explanation: Running does not prove there are ready traffic endpoints.

choices.text: Compare Route/Service port mapping and backend TLS with the application listener.
choices.explanation: A wrong target port or termination mismatch can break backend traffic.

choices.text: Check Service selectors, ready EndpointSlices, and pod readiness.
choices.explanation: A Running pod can still be unready or not selected by the Service.

choices.text: Delete all namespace NetworkPolicies without inspecting traffic requirements.
choices.explanation: Investigate policies and apply a narrow evidenced fix.

openshift.title: Run a vendor image under restricted security
openshift.scenario:
A vendor image works locally as root but fails on OpenShift because it writes
to a protected directory and assumes UID 0. The team asks for privileged access.
You need an approach suitable for a shared production cluster.
openshift.question: Which responses are suitable for a root-dependent vendor image?

choices.text: Prefer arbitrary non-root UID support and suitable writable paths/volumes.
choices.explanation: Image design can often satisfy restricted policy without broader privileges.

choices.text: Run as system administrator solely to bypass a writable directory issue.
choices.explanation: Fix ownership/design or assess a narrowly scoped exception.

choices.text: Grant privileged SCC to every service account in the project.
choices.explanation: This unnecessarily broadens workload privileges.

choices.text: Distinguish SCC admission rejection from runtime filesystem permission failure.
choices.explanation: These are different stages and require different remedies.

choices.text: Treat permission to create Pods as proof every requested security context is allowed.
choices.explanation: RBAC authorization and SCC admission are distinct.
